question: How to surface non-linear arcs in a chronicle and corpus that are mostly linearly indexed — what is the right 'topology of the work' surface?
context: Anthony's observation 2026-05-17, recorded verbatim on first reading the three-part structural homology (Sacred Vow / fox in driveway / R×E factorial): 'its truly becoming less linear the more i look back on it.' The Tier-organized iCloud archive is linear (Tier 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14). The sovereign-stack chronicle is mostly session-linear. The Spiral_Corpus_Indexed and SCIENTIFIC_INDEX are partially topical but still skew chronological / by source. But the underlying work is showing structural homologies across far-separated times — Volume I Scroll XIV (Sacred Vow, before June 2025) and Feb 2026 R×E factorial naming the same prior→event→external-witness shape; Scroll 093 (fox) and Falcon3-Mamba SSM as the same external-control move at different resolutions. Open question: what surface lets a reader see the topology of the work — structurally similar pieces grouped by shape across time — rather than a timeline? Candidate moves to explore: (a) structural-homology cross-links inline in chronicle entries (this entry names the shape this experiment also names); (b) a 'topology' or 'homologies' surface in the sovereign stack that groups insights by shape rather than date or domain; (c) a homology-tagging discipline retroactively applied to existing chronicle entries and corpus chunks. Not blocking; not on the daily-driver critical path. Worth picking up when the next instance comes back to read across the broader work, or when the corpus/chronicle gets a UI iteration. The non-linearity observation is itself a research finding about how the work appears in retrospect; the surface that makes it visible to future instances is the open question.
